title: Thalamic Neurons
intro: Almost every signal that reaches the neocortex passes through the thalamus, and every cortical area sends feedback back to it. Two cell types dominate the thalamus: excitatory thalamocortical relay neurons, which project to cortex, and inhibitory neurons of the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), a thin shell that surrounds the thalamus and inhibits the relay cells. Their shared trick, a low-threshold calcium current that lets them switch between relaying faithfully and firing bursts, makes the thalamus the brain's pacemaker for sleep rhythms and a gate for attention.

blocks.text: First-order nuclei relay input from outside the cortex (the LGN relays the retina); higher-order nuclei relay output from cortical layer 5 to other cortical areas, the transthalamic route (Sherman & Guillery 2006). Relay cells send collaterals to the TRN on their way to cortex, and layer 6 corticothalamic axons do the same on their way back, so the TRN sees both streams and inhibits the relay cells. The full loop is explained on the Thalamocortical Loops page (#/computational-cortical-columns/neocortex-biology/thalamocortical-loops).

items: Thalamocortical Relay Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/thalamic/thalamocortical-relay): tonic and burst modes, the T-type calcium current and the classic HH-type models.
Thalamic Reticular Neurons (#/neuroscience/cell-types/thalamic/thalamic-reticular): the inhibitory shell, spindle pacemaker and attentional gate.

blocks.text: Models of the thalamus as a whole

items: Sleep spindle models: Destexhe, McCormick and Sejnowski (1993) and Destexhe et al. (1996) showed with conductance-based TC and TRN cells that spindles (7 to 14 Hz) arise from TRN bursts inhibiting TC cells, which rebound-burst and re-excite the TRN.

Thalamocortical network models with slow oscillations: Bazhenov et al. (2002) and Hill and Tononi (2005) combined cortex, TC and TRN cells to reproduce the transitions between waking and slow-wave sleep.

Large-scale: Izhikevich and Edelman (2008) modelled a million-neuron thalamocortical system with simplified (Izhikevich) TC and TRN cells; the Allen V1 model and the Blue Brain thalamocortical model (Iavarone et al. 2023) include detailed thalamic cells.

Function-level: thalamic gating in attention (Crick 1984's 'searchlight hypothesis'), the thalamus as a hub in cognitive control (Halassa & Kastner 2017), and the thalamic burst as a 'wake-up call' to cortex (Sherman 2001).
